description: Breakout online free: steer the paddle, bounce the ball, and smash every brick. Three lives, faster balls on every level — how many bricks can you clear?
faq: How do I move the paddle?
Move the mouse, drag your finger across the game, or use Arrow Left and Arrow Right (or A and D). On a phone, drag your finger along the bottom of the screen.
How do I launch the ball?
Tap anywhere on the game, click, or press Space when the ball is sitting on the paddle. The ball flies off at a random angle, so be ready to catch it.
How do I control where the ball goes?

The ball bounces off the paddle at an angle that depends on where it lands: hit it with the middle and it goes straight up, hit it near an edge and it flies off at a sharp angle. Use the edges to reach the far corners of the wall.
How many points is each brick worth?
The top row is worth 50 points, then 40, 30, 20, and the bottom row 10. The higher bricks are worth more because they are harder to reach.
What happens when I clear every brick?
You reach the next level: a fresh wall appears and the ball flies a little faster. The speed keeps rising with every level.
How many lives do I get?
Three. You lose one each time the ball slips past the paddle. Lose all three and the game is over.

lede: The arcade original, in your browser. A wall of bright bricks, one bouncing ball, and a paddle at the bottom. Steer the paddle to keep the ball in play, smash every brick to clear the level, and watch the ball fly faster with each wall you break. The top row is worth the most points because it is the hardest to reach — and the edges of the paddle are your steering wheel, sending the ball off at sharp angles to hunt the far corners.

p: Press Start breaking and the ball sits on the paddle, waiting. Tap anywhere, click, or press Space to launch it. It flies up towards the wall of bricks, and every brick it touches shatters for points. Steer the paddle with the mouse, your finger, or the Arrow keys to catch the ball on its way back down.

If the ball slips past the paddle, you lose one of your three lives. Clear every brick and a fresh wall appears for the next level, with a faster ball. When all three lives are gone, you see your score, how many bricks you smashed, and which breaker rank that earns.

Each row of bricks is worth a different number of points: the top row is 50, then 40, 30, 20, and the bottom row 10. A full wall of 40 bricks is worth 1,200 points, so a perfect level is a big score — but the top rows only fall once the rows below them are gone, and the ball has to travel furthest to reach them.

The ball starts at about 265 pixels a second and speeds up by 30 pixels a second with every level you clear, up to about 480 pixels a second. The paddle never gets smaller, so the challenge is purely the pace: at level five the ball crosses the screen in under two seconds.

sections.h: From an Atari cabinet to your browser
p: Breakout was released by Atari in 1976, as a follow-up to Pong. Nolan Bushnell and Steve Bristow came up with the idea — a wall of bricks instead of a second player — and the prototype was famously built by a young Steve Wozniak, with Steve Jobs working alongside him, in four days of near-continuous work.

The game became one of the defining arcade cabinets of the late 1970s, and its idea has never gone away: every brick-breaker since, from the bundled games on early home computers to the paddle games on phones today, is a version of that same wall. The version here is the same idea, free in your browser, with a glowing paddle and a ball that leaves a trail of sparks.

ol: Catch the ball with the edge of the paddle, not the middle. An angled bounce reaches the top rows and the far corners that a straight bounce never touches.
Keep the paddle moving, not parked. Small, early moves put you under the ball sooner than one big correction at the last moment.
Clear the bottom rows first on purpose: once a gap opens, the ball slips through it and smashes the high-value top rows from above.
On a phone, drag with the finger of one hand and watch the ball, not the paddle. The paddle follows your finger, so your eyes should be on the ball.
Let the ball do the work on the top rows. A ball bouncing between the ceiling and the top row clears bricks on its own — just be ready when it comes back down.
